title: Special Populations, Extrication & Terrorism
summary: Patients whose bodies, brains, or hardware change how you assess and move them, plus the calls where the scene itself is the emergency: vehicle extrication, technical rescue, transport operations, and a chemical or explosive attack.

lessons.title: Developmental and intellectual disability, autism and how to communicate
lessons.body:
## The word "disability" hides three different problems

A patient can have trouble **thinking** (intellectual disability), trouble **moving** (cerebral palsy), or trouble **processing input** (autism). These are separate. Treating them as one blob is the single most common mistake on these calls, and it leads directly to under-assessing a patient who could have told you exactly what hurt.

Start from a rule that costs you nothing: **assume the patient understands you.** Speak to the patient first, then to the caregiver. Being nonverbal is not the same as being unable to comprehend.

### Intellectual and developmental disability

Intellectual disability means below-average reasoning plus trouble with daily living skills, present before age `18`. Severity is a spectrum; most people with it live and work with support and can answer simple questions accurately.

**Down syndrome** (trisomy 21) is the most common genetic cause. Two things matter to you physically. First, **atlantoaxial instability**: the ligament holding the first two neck bones together is lax in roughly `10-15%` of patients, so a small force can shift C1 on C2. Handle the neck gently and treat mechanism seriously. Second, the **airway**: large tongue, small mid-face, short neck, and narrow trachea. Consider a smaller airway adjunct than the patient's body size suggests. Congenital heart defects are present in about `50%` at birth.

**Cerebral palsy** is a movement disorder from an injury to the developing brain. Muscles are tight and joints may be permanently bent (contractures) — you cannot and must not straighten them to fit a stretcher. Pad the voids instead. Many patients with CP have completely normal intelligence and are simply hard to understand because the same brain injury affects the muscles of speech. Talk to them like adults.

### Autism spectrum disorder

Autism is a difference in how the brain handles social signals and sensory input. On a call, that shows up as: no eye contact, repeating your words back (echolalia), repetitive self-soothing movement (**stimming** — rocking, hand flapping), taking language completely literally, and being overwhelmed by lights, sirens, sound, and touch.

> **Trap:** No eye contact is not evasion, guilt, or altered mental status. Neither is a flat tone or an odd answer. Do not chart "uncooperative" for behavior that is the diagnosis.

Sensory overload is the thing you can actually fix. Kill the lightbar if the scene is safe, shut off the siren approaching, dim the box, drop your voice, and get everyone but one provider out of the patient's space.

### The communication playbook

- **One person talks.** Crowding a patient with three voices guarantees a meltdown.
- **Short, concrete sentences.** "I am going to touch your arm" beats "Do you mind if I take a quick look?" Avoid idioms — "I'll be right back in a second" is heard literally.
- **Announce before you touch.** Every time.
- **Ask the caregiver for the baseline.** "Is this how he normally talks?" turns an unanswerable mental status question into a usable one.
- **Allow the comfort object.** The blanket, the tablet, the stuffed animal rides along. It is a sedative you do not have to carry.
- **Give time.** Processing a question can take `10-15 seconds`. Silence is not refusal.

> **On the exam:** The correct answer on an autism question is almost always the one that reduces stimulation and involves the caregiver, not the one that restrains, sedates, or speeds up.
keyPoints: Assume the patient understands you; speak to the patient first, caregiver second.
Down syndrome: atlantoaxial instability (10-15%), large tongue and narrow airway, ~50% congenital heart defects.
Cerebral palsy affects movement, often not intelligence; pad around contractures instead of straightening them.
Autism: no eye contact, literal language and stimming are the diagnosis, not uncooperativeness.
Lower the lights and sirens, one person talks, short concrete sentences, allow the comfort object.

checks.q: A 9-year-old with Down syndrome fell from playground equipment onto his head. What anatomic concern raises your suspicion for spinal injury?
choices: Fused cervical vertebrae that crack under low force
Atlantoaxial instability, a lax ligament between C1 and C2
Absent cervical spinous processes
An enlarged foramen magnum
checks.why: Roughly 10-15% of patients with Down syndrome have a lax transverse ligament allowing C1 to shift on C2, so relatively low-force mechanisms can injure the cord. The vertebrae are not fused and the other options are not features of trisomy 21.

checks.q: An adult with cerebral palsy answers your questions with slurred, hard-to-understand speech. What should you assume?
choices: His cognition is likely intact and the speech muscles are affected
He has an intellectual disability and you should ask the caregiver instead
He is postictal from a seizure
He is intoxicated until proven otherwise
checks.why: The same brain injury that causes spasticity affects the muscles of speech; many patients with CP have normal intelligence. Redirecting to the caregiver without asking the patient discards your best source of history.

checks.q: Which set of actions best manages an autistic patient who is rocking, covering his ears, and not answering?
choices: Raise your voice, repeat the question faster, and hold his hands still
Apply soft restraints early to prevent escalation
Shut off the lightbar, have one provider speak in short sentences, and ask the caregiver about baseline
Transport immediately with lights and siren to shorten the exposure
checks.why: Rocking and ear-covering are sensory overload. Reducing stimulation, using a single calm voice, and getting baseline from the caregiver de-escalate it. Restraint, volume, and sirens all add input and worsen the reaction.

lessons.title: Hearing, vision and speech impairment on a call
lessons.body:
## The patient knows what is wrong; the channel is broken

Sensory impairment does not change your assessment. It changes how information gets between you and the patient. Fix the channel and the call becomes ordinary.

### Deaf and hard of hearing

About `15%` of American adults report some hearing loss. Two mechanisms: **conductive** (sound cannot get in — wax, fluid, a punctured eardrum) and **sensorineural** (the nerve or cochlea is damaged — age, noise, medications). Sensorineural loss is usually permanent and is what hearing aids and cochlear implants address.

What works:

- **Face the patient in good light** so lips and expression are visible. Do not turn away mid-sentence or talk from behind the stretcher.
- **Do not shout.** Shouting distorts the mouth shape and clips consonants. Speak normally, slightly slower, slightly lower in pitch.
- **Check for hearing aids** and bring them. A patient separated from a `2,000 dollar` hearing aid at the ED door is functionally isolated for the rest of the visit. Bring the charger for a cochlear implant processor if it is handy.
- **Write it down.** A pen and pad, or typing on a screen, is fast and accurate.
- **Ask about an interpreter.** American Sign Language is a distinct language with its own grammar, not English on the hands, and the hospital is legally obligated to provide an ASL interpreter. Note the need in your radio report so the ED can get one started.

> **Trap:** Do not assume lip reading works. Even skilled lip readers catch only about `30-40%` of English speech from the lips alone; the rest is guessed from context. A nodding patient may have understood nothing.

### Blindness and low vision

- **Announce yourself by name and role on entry** and say when you are moving away, or the patient is left talking to an empty room.
- **Narrate before you touch.** "I'm going to put a cuff on your right arm now."
- **Guide, do not push.** Offer your elbow and let the patient take your arm and walk half a step behind. Steering someone by the shoulders is disorienting.
- **Bring the white cane and the service animal.** A service dog is not a pet; it rides with the patient whenever it can be done safely. Do not pet or distract a working dog.

### Speech problems: three different things

| Problem | What broke | What it sounds like |
|---|---|---|
| Aphasia | Language centers in the brain (stroke) | Words are wrong or missing; comprehension may also be lost |
| Dysarthria | Muscles of speech (stroke, CP, ALS) | Slurred but the words chosen are correct |
| Intellectual impairment | Reasoning | Simple word choice, concrete answers, clear articulation |

Separating these matters. **Expressive aphasia** — the patient knows exactly what he wants and cannot get the word out — is terrifying for the patient and is a stroke finding. **Receptive aphasia** means your questions are not landing, and the fluent nonsense that comes back gets mistaken for psychiatric illness or intoxication.

### Laryngectomy and stoma speech

A patient whose voice box was removed breathes through a permanent hole in the neck (a **stoma**) and may speak with an electrolarynx held to the neck, or by swallowed-air (esophageal) speech. The mouth and nose no longer connect to the lungs. If this patient needs ventilation, you ventilate the stoma — not the face.

> **On shift:** Whatever the impairment, document how you communicated. "History obtained in writing" or "ASL interpreter via video at bedside" tells the next provider the information is reliable.
keyPoints: Face the patient, speak normally, never shout; shouting distorts the mouth and consonants.
Lip reading captures only 30-40% of speech, so a nod is not confirmation of understanding.
Bring hearing aids, canes, and service animals with the patient; request an ASL interpreter early.
Aphasia is language (a stroke finding), dysarthria is muscles, intellectual impairment is reasoning.
A laryngectomy patient breathes and is ventilated through the neck stoma, not the face.

checks.q: Your 78-year-old patient is hard of hearing. Which technique is most effective?
choices: Shout each question directly into the better ear
Speak only to the family member who called 911
Face him in good light, speak at a normal volume slightly slower, and offer a pen and pad
Assume he can lip-read and remove your view of his face to work faster
checks.why: Facing the patient preserves lip and facial cues; shouting distorts mouth shape and clips consonants. Bypassing the patient discards history, and lip reading alone catches only about 30-40% of speech.

checks.q: A patient who had a stroke understands you perfectly but cannot produce the word he wants. This is:
choices: Expressive aphasia
Dysarthria
Receptive aphasia
An intellectual disability
checks.why: Expressive aphasia is intact comprehension with blocked output. Dysarthria is slurred articulation with correct word choice, receptive aphasia is lost comprehension with fluent but wrong speech, and intellectual disability does not appear suddenly after a stroke.

checks.q: A patient with a laryngectomy becomes apneic. How do you ventilate?
choices: BVM to the face with the stoma occluded
Mouth-to-mouth with the nose pinched
Nasal cannula at 15 L/min
Ventilate through the neck stoma, using a pediatric mask or attaching the BVM directly
checks.why: After a laryngectomy the upper airway no longer connects to the lungs, so face ventilation moves no air. A pediatric mask seals well over the stoma, or the BVM can connect directly to a trach tube in the stoma.

lessons.title: Technology-dependent patients: tracheostomies and home ventilators
lessons.body:
## Machines in the living room

Patients who would once have lived in an ICU now live at home. Two pieces of hardware account for most of your bad calls: the tracheostomy and the home ventilator.

### Tracheostomy anatomy

A tracheostomy is a surgical opening through the front of the neck into the trachea, usually between the second and third tracheal rings, held open by a tube. Air now bypasses the nose and mouth entirely, so it arrives **cold, dry, and unfiltered** — which is exactly why these tubes clog with thick secretions.

- **Cuffed vs uncuffed.** A cuff is a small balloon that seals the trachea so a ventilator can push pressure in without leaking. Cuffed tubes are common in ventilated adults. Uncuffed tubes are usual in children (the cricoid already seals) and in patients who talk, because air must slip past the tube to reach the vocal cords.
- **Inner cannula.** Many adult tubes have a removable inner sleeve. If the tube is obstructed, **pull the inner cannula first** — it is often the plug itself, and removing it takes three seconds and no skill.
- **Obturator.** The smooth plug used to insert the tube. Families keep it taped to the wall; it matters only for reinsertion.

### Suctioning

Suctioning clears the tube. It also strips oxygen out of the lungs and can trigger bradycardia via vagal stimulation, so it is timed.

- **Preoxygenate** for `30-60 seconds` with high-flow oxygen or several BVM breaths first.
- **Insert without suction applied**, only to the length of the tube (or to a pre-measured depth the family knows) — do not jam the catheter in blind.
- **Apply suction while withdrawing, rotating the catheter.**
- **Suction no longer than `10 seconds`** in an adult (`5 seconds` in an infant), then reoxygenate for `30 seconds` before the next pass.
- A few mL of sterile saline may be instilled to loosen a plug where protocol allows.

> **Key:** `10 seconds` and out. If the patient desaturates during a pass, stop immediately and ventilate.

### When a ventilated patient goes bad: DOPE

| Letter | Problem | What you do |
|---|---|---|
| **D** | Displacement — tube out of the trachea or into a mainstem | Look, listen, reposition, prepare to reinsert or bag the stoma |
| **O** | Obstruction — mucus plug | Remove inner cannula, suction |
| **P** | Pneumothorax | Unequal chest rise, absent breath sounds, rising pressures — rapid transport |
| **E** | Equipment failure — circuit, power, oxygen out | Disconnect and bag |

Work it in order. The first two cover most of what you will actually see.

### If the trach is obstructed and will not clear

Remove the inner cannula, suction once, and if there is still no air movement, **disconnect from the machine and ventilate with a BVM attached directly to the trach tube** at `15 L/min` oxygen. If the tube itself is plugged solid or has come out, ventilate the stoma with an infant or pediatric mask sealed over the neck opening — and if the patient still has an intact upper airway (a tracheostomy, not a laryngectomy), BVM the face while sealing the stoma with a gloved hand works as a backup.

### Home ventilators

Families know their machine better than you do. Ask them. What you must recognize are the alarms:

- **High-pressure alarm** — something is resisting flow: a mucus plug, a kinked circuit, the patient biting or coughing, bronchospasm, or a pneumothorax.
- **Low-pressure or low-volume alarm** — air is escaping: a disconnected circuit, a leaking or deflated cuff, or a tube that has come out.
- **Apnea alarm** — no patient effort detected on a spontaneous mode.

> **On shift:** You are never obligated to troubleshoot a ventilator. The universal EMT answer to a deteriorating ventilated patient is: **disconnect from the vent, bag the tube with 100% oxygen, and reassess.** That removes the machine from the differential in one move.

Bring the home equipment — spare trach tubes (same size and one size smaller), suction unit, and the vent settings sheet — with the patient.
keyPoints: Suction no longer than 10 seconds in an adult (5 in an infant), preoxygenate 30-60 seconds before and after.
Insert the catheter with no suction applied; suction while withdrawing and rotating.
DOPE: Displacement, Obstruction, Pneumothorax, Equipment — in that order.
Pull the inner cannula first on an obstructed trach; it is often the plug.
Deteriorating ventilated patient: disconnect from the vent and bag with oxygen at 15 L/min.

checks.q: How long may you apply suction during a single pass in an adult tracheostomy patient?
choices: 30 seconds
20 seconds
No more than 10 seconds
As long as secretions keep returning
checks.why: Suctioning removes oxygen along with secretions and can cause vagally mediated bradycardia. Ten seconds maximum in an adult, five in an infant, with reoxygenation between passes; unlimited suctioning is how patients desaturate and arrest.

checks.q: A home ventilator sounds a high-pressure alarm and the patient's chest is barely moving. Which DOPE causes fit best?
choices: Circuit disconnection or a deflated cuff
Mucus plug obstruction or a pneumothorax
Power failure of the ventilator
The apnea alarm threshold is set too high
checks.why: High pressure means resistance to flow: obstruction or pneumothorax. Disconnections and cuff leaks cause LOW pressure alarms, and a power failure would silence or change the machine rather than alarm high.

checks.q: Your first action on an obstructed tracheostomy tube is to:
choices: Remove the entire trach tube and ventilate the bare stoma
Instill 10 mL of saline and wait
Begin chest compressions
Remove the inner cannula, then suction
checks.why: The inner cannula is frequently the obstruction itself and removing it is immediate and low risk. Pulling the whole tube is a later step if that fails, large saline volumes are not indicated, and compressions are not indicated in a patient with a pulse.

lessons.title: Feeding tubes, central lines, VP shunts and ostomies
lessons.body:
## Hardware you will meet and what goes wrong with it

You do not manage these devices. You recognize the failure and protect the patient while you transport. Every one of these has a characteristic emergency.

### Feeding tubes

**NG / OG tubes** run through the nose or mouth to the stomach. Short-term. They can be dislodged into the airway, and a tube that has migrated up makes vomiting and aspiration more likely.

**Gastrostomy (G-tube)** goes through the abdominal wall directly into the stomach; a **PEG** is a G-tube placed endoscopically. A **J-tube** goes into the jejunum, past the stomach, for patients who aspirate their feeds.

What goes wrong:

- **Dislodged tube.** The tract can start closing within hours. Do not attempt to reinsert unless your protocol says so; cover the site with a dry dressing and transport. Save the tube and bring it.
- **Clogged tube.** Uncomfortable, not an emergency. Transport.
- **Leaking around the site** with red, weeping skin — irritation, sometimes infection.
- **Aspiration.** The real killer. Tube-fed patients are often supine and neurologically impaired. Suction, position on the side if you can, oxygenate.
- **Bleeding or a swollen, painful abdomen** around the site.

Key assessment habit: **stop the feed** before you transport a vomiting or distressed tube-fed patient, and transport with the head elevated `30 degrees` unless the spine or pressure says otherwise.

### Central venous lines, PICCs, and ports

A **central line** ends in the large veins near the heart. A **PICC** enters at the upper arm and threads centrally. An **implanted port** sits under the skin of the chest as a small disc and is accessed with a special needle.

Three emergencies:

1. **Infection.** A central line is a highway from skin to bloodstream. Fever plus redness, warmth, or drainage at the site in a line patient means sepsis until proven otherwise.
2. **Bleeding.** Direct pressure. These lines sit in high-flow vessels.
3. **Air embolism.** If a line is open to the air — a cracked hub, a disconnected cap — the negative pressure of a breath can pull air in. **Clamp the line, cover the site, and place the patient on the left side with the head down (left lateral Trendelenburg)**, which traps the air bubble in the right ventricle instead of letting it into the pulmonary circulation. Give high-flow oxygen.

> **Trap:** Do not use a central line, port, or PICC for your own access. That is outside EMT scope and outside most paramedic protocols without specific training.

### VP shunts

A **ventriculoperitoneal shunt** drains cerebrospinal fluid from a ventricle in the brain, under the skin behind the ear, down the neck and chest, into the abdomen. You can often feel the tubing as a cord along the neck. When it blocks, disconnects, or infects, pressure builds inside the skull.

Shunt failure signs: **headache, vomiting, sleepiness or irritability, and altered mental status** — with fever if it is infected. In an infant, look for a **bulging, tense fontanelle**, high-pitched cry, poor feeding, and sunset eyes.

Late rising intracranial pressure produces **Cushing's triad**: rising blood pressure with a widening pulse pressure, **slowing** heart rate, and irregular breathing. That combination is a brain about to herniate. Transport to a facility with neurosurgery, head elevated `30 degrees`, oxygenate, and ventilate at a normal rate — do not hyperventilate routinely.

> **Key:** In a shunt patient, headache plus vomiting plus "not acting right" is a surgical emergency, not a stomach bug.

### Ostomies

A surgically created opening that diverts waste to a bag on the abdomen. A **colostomy** drains formed stool from the colon, an **ileostomy** drains liquid, caustic output from the small intestine, and a **urostomy** drains urine. Ileostomy patients dehydrate fast because they lose fluid the colon would normally reabsorb.

Handle the bag gently, do not remove the appliance, and protect the patient's dignity — keep it covered. A stoma should look pink and moist; dusky or black is dead bowel and is an emergency.

### In passing

**Implanted pain pumps** (intrathecal) deliver drugs into the spinal fluid; a malfunction can mean overdose or sudden withdrawal. **Vagal nerve stimulators** for epilepsy sit under the left collarbone with a magnet the patient swipes over it to abort a seizure; ask the family where the magnet is.
keyPoints: A dislodged G-tube tract can start closing within hours: cover it, bring the tube, do not force reinsertion.
Aspiration is the main killer in tube-fed patients; stop the feed and transport head up 30 degrees.
Suspected air embolism from a central line: clamp, cover, left lateral with head down, high-flow oxygen.
Shunt failure equals headache, vomiting, altered mental status; in infants a bulging fontanelle.
Cushing's triad is rising BP, slowing pulse, irregular breathing — rising intracranial pressure.

checks.q: An 8-month-old with a VP shunt is vomiting, lethargic, and has a tense, bulging fontanelle. This most likely indicates:
choices: Shunt failure with rising intracranial pressure
Viral gastroenteritis
Dehydration from poor feeding
A normal finding while crying
checks.why: Blocked CSF drainage raises intracranial pressure, producing vomiting, altered mental status, and a bulging fontanelle. Gastroenteritis and dehydration cause a sunken, not tense, fontanelle, and a bulging fontanelle in a quiet infant is never normal.

checks.q: A home health patient's central line cap has come off and she suddenly becomes short of breath and hypotensive. Best immediate action?
choices: Flush the line with saline to clear it
Sit her fully upright and reassure her
Clamp the line, cover the site, place her left side down with head lowered, and give high-flow oxygen
Withdraw the line completely and apply a tourniquet
checks.why: This is an air embolism. Clamping stops further entrainment and left lateral head-down traps air in the right ventricle. Flushing pushes air onward, sitting upright speeds it toward the pulmonary outflow, and EMTs do not remove central lines.

checks.q: Which ostomy patient is at highest risk of rapid dehydration?
choices: Colostomy, because stool is formed
Urostomy, because urine is diverted
None; ostomies do not affect fluid balance
Ileostomy, because liquid output bypasses the colon's reabsorption
checks.why: The colon reabsorbs most water from stool. An ileostomy drains before that happens, so output is liquid and high-volume. Colostomy output is formed, and a urostomy diverts urine the kidneys already produced.

lessons.title: Bariatric patients, hospice, DNR and POLST
lessons.body:
## Two calls where the hard part is not clinical

### The bariatric patient

Bariatric generally means a body weight over about `300 pounds` or a BMI over `40`. The medicine is ordinary. The physics and the dignity are not.

**Logistics first, and early.** A standard stretcher is rated around `500-650 pounds`; bariatric stretchers go to `1,000-1,600 pounds`. Exceeding the rating is how crews and patients end up on the floor. Call for a bariatric unit and extra hands **before** you move anything — a safe lift usually needs `4-6` people plus a plan for stairs, doorways, and the ramp. Use a tarp or bariatric slide sheet, keep the load close, and never improvise by using bedsheets that tear.

**Physiology that bites:**

- **Positioning.** Lying flat lets abdominal contents press on the diaphragm, so breathing gets worse supine. Transport in a semi-Fowler's or ramped position unless you have a reason not to.
- **Airway.** Excess soft tissue means a harder mask seal and a shorter safe apnea time. Two-person BVM early.
- **Obesity hypoventilation syndrome.** Chronically retained carbon dioxide means these patients may run a lower baseline oxygen saturation and may be on home CPAP or BiPAP.
- **Blood pressure cuff.** A cuff too small reads falsely high. The bladder should cover about `80%` of arm circumference — use a large adult or thigh cuff, or measure at the forearm and document where.
- **Assessment.** Lung sounds are muffled, pulses are hard to find, and landmarks disappear. Rely more on respiratory rate, effort, and mental status.

> **On shift:** Say nothing about the patient's weight beyond what the chart needs. Discuss the lift plan away from the patient. These patients avoid calling 911 because of how they have been treated before, and they arrive sicker for it.

### Hospice, palliative care, and the end of life

**Palliative care** is comfort-focused treatment that can run alongside curative treatment, at any stage. **Hospice** is palliative care for someone with a prognosis measured in about `6 months` or less, where curative treatment has stopped. Both are active medicine. Neither means "do nothing."

Hospice patients call 911 for real reasons: uncontrolled pain, a fall, a distressed caregiver, a device problem. Your first move is the phone: **hospice has a 24-hour nurse line**, and the hospice nurse can often resolve it without a transport the patient never wanted.

### DNR, DNAR, POLST

A **DNR** (do not resuscitate; DNAR, do not attempt resuscitation) is a physician order that says: if the heart stops and breathing stops, do not start CPR.

What a DNR is **not**: it is not a refusal of care. A DNR patient still gets oxygen, suctioning, pain control, splinting, bleeding control, positioning, and transport. It applies at cardiac arrest, not before it.

**POLST / MOLST** (Physician/Medical Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment; New Jersey uses **POLST**) is a broader, portable medical order set on a brightly colored form, signed by the patient or their representative and a physician, APN, or PA. It covers CPR, the level of intervention wanted (comfort-focused, limited, full), artificial nutrition, and antibiotics. It travels with the patient between home, nursing facility, and hospital.

To honor an out-of-hospital DNR you generally need: the **original or a valid state-recognized copy** (or an approved bracelet/necklace), the patient **identifiable** as the person named, and the form **signed and not expired or revoked**. Rules vary by state, so know your protocol.

> **Trap:** When you cannot find the form, cannot confirm it applies, or the situation is genuinely unclear, **begin resuscitation** and contact medical control. You can stop; you cannot un-delay.

**When family reverses the DNR at the bedside** — "do everything" from a grieving spouse — the safe path in most systems is to begin resuscitation and take it to medical control immediately, rather than argue over a body on the living room floor. A patient can revoke their own DNR verbally at any time.

**At the deathbed**, do the small things: say what is happening in plain words, let family touch the patient, do not narrate the monitor, and offer to call clergy or hospice. Document the form, its number if it has one, who was present, and the time.
keyPoints: Standard stretchers rate around 500-650 lb; bariatric units 1,000-1,600 lb. Call for resources before lifting.
Transport bariatric patients semi-upright; supine worsens breathing, and an undersized BP cuff reads falsely high.
Hospice means prognosis about 6 months or less; call the 24-hour hospice nurse line first.
A DNR blocks CPR at arrest only — oxygen, suction, pain control, and transport still apply.
Unclear, missing, or contested DNR: start resuscitation and contact medical control.

checks.q: Your patient has a valid out-of-hospital DNR and is awake, in pain from a hip fracture. What care is appropriate?
choices: None; the DNR prohibits treatment and transport
Comfort measures only, with no transport offered
Full assessment, oxygen if indicated, splinting, positioning for comfort, and transport
Wait on scene for the patient to arrest before acting
checks.why: A DNR only withholds resuscitation at cardiac and respiratory arrest. It never withholds assessment, oxygen, splinting, comfort care, or transport. The patient is awake with a treatable injury.

checks.q: Why does a blood pressure cuff that is too small produce a misleading reading on a bariatric patient?
choices: It reads falsely low because it cannot compress the artery
It reads falsely high because more pressure is needed to occlude the artery
It has no effect as long as the pulse is palpable
It only affects the diastolic number
checks.why: An undersized bladder must be inflated to higher pressure to compress the brachial artery through the tissue, so both numbers read high. The bladder should span about 80% of arm circumference.

checks.q: You arrive at a hospice home. The patient is in cardiac arrest, the POLST says 'Do Not Attempt Resuscitation,' and the daughter screams to do everything. Best action in most systems?
choices: Refuse to touch the patient and wait for the medical examiner
Remove the daughter from the room and honor the form without discussion
Ask the daughter to sign a refusal and leave
Begin resuscitation and contact medical control immediately
checks.why: A contested or revoked directive at the bedside is resolved by starting care and going to medical control, because resuscitation can be stopped but lost time cannot be recovered. Arguing with family over a body or leaving the scene are both indefensible.

lessons.title: Abuse and neglect: children, elders and intimate partners
lessons.body:
## You are often the only outsider who sees the house

Nurses see the patient. You see the environment, the other people, the food in the fridge, and the story before anyone has rehearsed it. That makes EMS uniquely positioned — and legally obligated — to notice.

### The four categories

**Physical, sexual, emotional abuse, and neglect.** Neglect is the most common and the most missed: untreated bedsores, missing medications, filthy clothing, no food, an untended diaper, a child left to a sibling.

### Child abuse: the findings that should stop you

- **Injuries in a non-mobile infant.** A child who cannot roll, crawl, or cruise does not bruise himself. "Those who don't cruise rarely bruise."
- **Patterned injuries.** A burn shaped like a cigarette tip, an iron, or a looped cord. Bite marks. Bruises in the shape of a hand or belt buckle.
- **Immersion burns.** A **stocking-and-glove** pattern — a sharp, level line around the ankles or wrists with no splash marks — means a limb was held in hot water. Real accidental scalds splash and have irregular edges. Doughnut-shaped sparing on the buttocks means the child was pressed against a cooler tub bottom.
- **Bruises in different stages of healing**, or bruises on the torso, ears, or neck (the **TEN** regions) in a child under `4`.
- **A story that does not fit the injury** — a skull fracture blamed on a `2-foot` fall off a couch — or a story that changes between tellers.
- **Delayed presentation.** Hours or days between the injury and the call.
- **Abusive head trauma** (shaken baby): an infant who is irritable, vomiting, seizing, or unresponsive with **no external signs of trauma**. Shaking tears bridging veins, causing subdural bleeding and retinal hemorrhages. Suspect it in any infant with unexplained altered mental status.

> **Trap:** Mongolian spots (congenital dermal melanocytosis — blue-gray flat patches over the lower back and buttocks) and the marks of cupping or coining are commonly mistaken for abuse. Ask before you accuse.

### Elder abuse

Older adults are abused by caregivers, adult children, and facilities. Look for: pressure ulcers that have been allowed to progress, dehydration and weight loss, over- or under-medication, unexplained fractures, fear of the caregiver, and a caregiver who answers every question for a competent patient and will not leave the room.

**Financial exploitation** is the most common form — a missing pension check, a suddenly changed will, unpaid bills in a home with income. It is reportable, and you may be the one who notices.

### Intimate partner violence

Injuries that do not match the story, injuries to the face, neck, and forearms (defensive), a partner who hovers, and a patient who minimizes. Strangulation is a specific red flag: hoarseness, neck pain, petechiae above the neck, or trouble swallowing — it predicts later homicide and needs transport even when it looks minor.

How to conduct the interview safely:

- **Separate the parties.** Take the patient to the ambulance for "a blood pressure." It is the only reliable way to get a private conversation.
- **Do not confront the suspected abuser.** Confrontation risks your safety and escalates the violence after you leave.
- **Do not promise secrecy** you cannot keep. Say what you will document and report.
- Ask simple, direct, non-judgmental questions. Accept the answer you get; disclosure often takes several encounters.

### Reporting, documentation, and evidence

EMTs are **mandatory reporters** of suspected child abuse in every state. The standard is **reasonable suspicion**, not proof — you do not investigate, you report. In **New Jersey**, suspected child abuse or neglect is reported to the State Central Registry hotline, `1-877-NJ-ABUSE` (`1-877-652-2873`), and the duty is on the individual who suspects it. Elder and vulnerable-adult reporting pathways exist as well; know your agency's. Reporting in good faith carries immunity; failing to report can be a crime.

**Document objectively.** Write what you saw, measured, and heard, in quotation marks when it is a statement. "Circular 1 cm burn to left forearm; mother states child 'grabbed the stove.'" Never write "child abuse" as a conclusion or name a suspect.

**Preserve evidence.** Cut around, not through, holes in clothing. Do not wash the patient. Discourage a sexual assault patient from bathing, changing, eating, or drinking, and bring clothing in a **paper**, not plastic, bag.

> **Key:** Scene safety outranks all of it. If the abuser is present and escalating, you stage, you call police, and you do not fix it yourself.
keyPoints: Injuries in a non-mobile infant, patterned burns, and stories that change are the core red flags.
Stocking-and-glove burns with a sharp line and no splash mean forced immersion.
Abusive head trauma can present as an unresponsive infant with no external injury.
Separate the parties to interview, never confront the abuser, never promise secrecy.
EMTs are mandatory reporters on reasonable suspicion; in NJ call 1-877-NJ-ABUSE. Document objectively.

checks.q: A 2-year-old has scald burns to both feet with a sharp, level line at the ankles and no splash marks. This pattern suggests:
choices: An accidental spill of hot liquid
A chemical rather than thermal burn
Forced immersion in hot water
A normal sunburn distribution
checks.why: Accidental spills splash and produce irregular, feathered edges. A sharp, level demarcation with no splash means the limbs were held in hot liquid. Chemical burns do not respect a waterline, and sunburn does not blister in a stocking pattern.

checks.q: You suspect intimate partner violence. The partner insists on riding in the back. What is the best approach?
choices: Confront the partner directly about the injuries
Take the patient alone to the ambulance for vitals and ask privately, without promising secrecy
Promise the patient that nothing said will be documented
Cancel transport and let police handle it
checks.why: Separation creates the only realistic chance of disclosure. Confrontation endangers you and the patient after you leave, secrecy is a promise you cannot keep, and cancelling transport abandons a patient with injuries.

checks.q: What legal standard triggers an EMT's duty to report suspected child abuse?
choices: Proof beyond a reasonable doubt
A confession by the caregiver
Physician confirmation at the hospital
Reasonable suspicion
checks.why: Mandatory reporting is triggered by reasonable suspicion, and good-faith reports are protected by immunity. Waiting for proof, a confession, or a physician's agreement delays protection and can itself be a crime.

lessons.title: Vehicle extrication: scene, stabilization, access and rapid extrication
lessons.body:
## Extrication is a process, not a tool

You are not the cutting crew. You are the person who keeps the patient alive inside a machine while other people take it apart, and who decides when the clock beats the spine.

### The phases

1. **Scene size-up and hazard control** — traffic, fire, fuel, power lines, the bystanders.
2. **Stabilization** — stop the vehicle from moving.
3. **Gaining access** — get to the patient.
4. **Disentanglement** — remove the vehicle from the patient, not the patient from the vehicle.
5. **Removal / packaging** — move the patient out on a device.
6. **Transport.**

### Hazards

**Traffic kills responders.** Park upstream in a fend-off (blocking) position, wear the ANSI-compliant high-visibility vest required on any federally funded roadway, and let fire or police own the lane. Turn off headlights pointed at oncoming traffic at night so you do not blind drivers into you.

**Fire and fuel.** A charged hose line is standard on a working extrication. Turn the vehicle off, and where accessible, disconnect the battery — negative first.

**Undeployed airbags.** An airbag that did not fire in the crash can still fire during extrication and will strike whoever is in its path. Never place your body, your head, or a tool between an undeployed bag and the patient. The common working rule is the **5-10-20 rule**: stay at least `5 inches` from a side-impact bag, `10 inches` from a driver bag, and `20 inches` from a passenger bag. Do not cut a pillar without knowing whether a curtain bag inflator runs through it.

**Hybrid and electric vehicles.** High-voltage cables are **orange** and may carry `200-800 volts` DC. Do not cut orange. Batteries damaged in a crash can enter **thermal runaway** — reignition hours or days later, extreme heat, and toxic vapor. Treat a smoking or hissing battery pack as a fire regardless of visible flame, and get the vehicle's emergency response guide if available.

**Stabilization.** A car on four inflated tires still rocks, and every rock moves an unstable spine. Crews build **cribbing** (interlocking wood) and **step chocks** against the rocker panels and may deflate the tires to settle the vehicle onto them. A vehicle on its side or roof gets struts. Nothing enters the car until it stops moving.

### Access

**Simple access** requires no tools: try every door, roll down a window, have a conscious patient unlock it. Try the doors first — it is free and it works more often than trainees expect.

**Complex access** requires tools and training: spreaders, cutters, rams, a door popped at the Nader pin, a roof flapped, a dash rolled.

**Glass.** Side and rear windows are **tempered** — they shatter into blunt cubes when struck at a lower corner with a spring-loaded center punch. The **windshield is laminated**: two layers of glass bonded to a plastic sheet, so it does not shatter and must be cut out with a saw or glass hook. Before any glass work, **cover the patient with a heavy blanket and protect their eyes and airway**, and put eye protection on yourself.

> **On shift:** Your job inside the car is small and enormous: manual in-line stabilization of the head, an airway, high-flow oxygen, bleeding control, constant reassurance, and telling the rescue officer what the patient's condition is doing. The patient hears everything. Narrate.

### Rapid extrication

Normally the patient comes out slowly and packaged. **Rapid extrication** skips the device and moves the patient directly onto a long board or stretcher with manual spinal control, in under a minute. It is justified in exactly three situations:

1. **The scene is unsafe** — fire, fuel, unstable structure, rising water, violence.
2. **The patient is unstable** — airway you cannot control in the seat, uncontrolled bleeding, shock, deteriorating mental status.
3. **The patient blocks access to a more critical patient.**

Comfort, impatience, and a long ETA are not on the list.

The classic technique takes **three rescuers**: one maintains manual in-line stabilization of the head from behind or beside, one rotates the patient's torso in controlled `1/8`-turn increments while a third moves the legs, and the patient is lowered onto the board and slid up. One person — usually the one at the head — calls every move.

> **On the exam:** Spinal motion restriction has narrowed a lot, but a long backboard is still the tool for **moving** a patient with a concerning mechanism out of a car, and boards are commonly removed once the patient is on the stretcher. The board is an extrication device more than a treatment.
keyPoints: Phases: size-up, stabilization, access, disentanglement, removal, transport — nothing enters until the car stops moving.
Undeployed airbags: 5 inches from side, 10 from driver, 20 from passenger bags; never sit in the deployment path.
Orange cables are high voltage on hybrids and EVs; damaged packs can enter thermal runaway hours later.
Side and rear glass is tempered and can be punched; the windshield is laminated and must be cut.
Rapid extrication only for an unsafe scene, an unstable patient, or blocked access to a worse patient.

checks.q: Which finding by itself justifies rapid extrication?
choices: The patient is anxious and wants out of the car
Fuel is pooling under the vehicle and vapor is visible
The receiving trauma center is 30 minutes away
The driver's door is jammed and fire is still en route
checks.why: An unsafe scene, an unstable patient, or blocked access to a more critical patient are the three criteria. Pooling fuel is an immediate scene hazard. Anxiety, transport distance, and a jammed door are inconveniences, not criteria.

checks.q: You need to break a window to reach a patient. Which one and why?
choices: The windshield, because it is largest
Any window; all automotive glass behaves the same
A side or rear window, because tempered glass shatters into blunt cubes when punched at a corner
The sunroof, because it is laminated and safest
checks.why: Side and rear windows are tempered and break cleanly with a center punch at a lower corner. The windshield is laminated safety glass bonded to plastic and must be cut out, which is slower and showers the patient with debris.

checks.q: During extrication you notice an undeployed side-impact airbag in the B-pillar. What is the correct response?
choices: Cut the pillar quickly before it can deploy
Deploy it manually by striking it
Ignore it; bags cannot fire after a crash
Keep at least 5 inches of clearance and keep yourself and tools out of its path
checks.why: Undeployed bags retain stored energy and can fire during extrication. The 5-10-20 inch rule keeps rescuers out of the deployment path; cutting a pillar that houses an inflator or deliberately striking a bag are both dangerous.

lessons.title: Rescue awareness: water, ice, confined space, trench and wilderness
lessons.body:
## The three levels, and why you stop at the first

Technical rescue training is tiered:

- **Awareness** — recognize the hazard, secure the scene, call the right resource, keep everyone out. This is where most EMTs sit.
- **Operations** — work at the edge of the hazard zone under a trained plan.
- **Technician** — enter and perform the rescue.

The reason this matters is a statistic, not a policy: in confined space incidents, a large share of the dead are **would-be rescuers** who went in after the first victim. A dead EMT does not treat anyone.

### Water rescue

The sequence, in order of increasing risk to you: **Reach, Throw, Row, Go.** Reach with an object from shore. Throw a rope or flotation. Row a boat. Only a trained, equipped swimmer goes.

Wear a personal flotation device any time you work within about `10 feet` of the water's edge.

**Cold water changes the rules.** Immersion below roughly `70 F` (`21 C`) triggers a cold shock gasp reflex, then rapidly stealing dexterity and strength over the first `10-15 minutes`. But the **mammalian diving reflex** — cold water on the face shunting blood to the brain and heart and dropping metabolism, strongest in children — means patients have survived submersion of `30 minutes` or more in very cold water with intact neurology. So: **begin resuscitation on a cold-water submersion victim and keep going.** "Not dead until warm and dead."

Self-rescue if you end up in the water: the **HELP position** (Heat Escape Lessening Posture) — knees drawn to the chest, arms pressed to the sides, floating still in a PFD. Swimming burns heat you cannot spare.

**Swiftwater foot entrapment** kills competent swimmers. A foot wedged between rocks in moving water, and the current folds the body forward and holds the face under. Never stand up or wade in moving water above the knee. If swept downstream, float on your back, feet first and pointed downstream, to fend off rocks.

### Ice rescue

Ice thickness is unpredictable; never trust it. Reach or throw from shore, use a ladder, rope, or inflatable to spread weight, and keep the victim's arms over the ice edge while a trained team works. Victims are frequently hypothermic and must be handled gently — rough movement of a very cold heart can trigger ventricular fibrillation.

### Confined space

A confined space has limited entry and exit and is not designed for continuous occupancy: silos, manholes, tanks, grain bins, cisterns. The killer is usually the atmosphere. Normal air is `21%` oxygen; an atmosphere below **`19.5%` oxygen is oxygen-deficient** by OSHA definition and can drop a person in one breath. Hydrogen sulfide, methane, carbon monoxide, and displaced oxygen from decomposition or inert gas are all common.

Entry is **permit-required**: atmospheric monitoring, ventilation, supplied-air respirators, a harness and retrieval line, and an attendant outside. **You do not enter.** If someone collapsed inside and a second person collapsed going after him, that is a confirmed atmospheric hazard, not a coincidence.

### Trench collapse

Soil weighs roughly `100 pounds` per cubic foot — a cubic yard is about `2,700 pounds`, the weight of a small car. A buried worker cannot expand his chest to breathe under it. **Secondary collapse** is extremely likely and is what kills rescuers.

Rules: no entry without engineered shoring, keep everyone and every vehicle back from the lip (spoil piles and heavy equipment vibration cause the next collapse), shut down machinery, and call a technical rescue team. Provide oxygen and reassurance from the surface if the victim's head is exposed.

### Structure collapse, rope and wilderness

**Structure collapse** brings voids, unstable debris, dust, and utilities. Stage; do not climb the pile.

**Low-angle rope** work is under about `40-45 degrees`, where the ground carries most of the load and ropes assist. **High-angle** is steeper than that, where the rope holds essentially all the weight and only technicians operate.

**Wilderness and search and rescue** add distance and time. Patient care runs for hours, not minutes: think hypothermia, hydration, splinting that must last, and a litter carry that needs `6-8` people per team with rotations.

> **Key:** At every one of these calls your real job is the same — stage in a safe area, set up to treat the patient the moment the technicians deliver him, manage the landing zone and the resources, and stay out of the hole.
keyPoints: Reach, Throw, Row, Go — in that order; wear a PFD within 10 feet of the water.
Cold-water submersion: resuscitate and keep going, the diving reflex allows survival past 30 minutes.
An atmosphere below 19.5% oxygen is oxygen-deficient; confined space entry is permit-required and not yours.
Soil is about 100 lb per cubic foot and secondary collapse kills rescuers — no trench entry without shoring.
Awareness level means secure, call the right team, and treat at the edge — never enter.

checks.q: A worker collapses in a manhole and his coworker collapses attempting rescue. What does this pattern tell you?
choices: Both likely had medical emergencies by coincidence
An oxygen-deficient or toxic atmosphere is present and no one enters without supplied air
The second victim tripped and struck his head
It is safe to enter briefly if you hold your breath
checks.why: Sequential collapse of a rescuer is the classic signature of a toxic or oxygen-deficient atmosphere (below 19.5% oxygen). Holding your breath does not protect against gases already displacing oxygen, and rescuers make up a large share of confined-space deaths.

checks.q: A child is pulled from an icy pond after 25 minutes of submersion and is pulseless. What is the correct approach?
choices: Withhold resuscitation; the downtime is incompatible with survival
Perform compressions for 2 minutes only, then stop
Warm the patient completely before starting compressions
Begin full resuscitation and continue during transport
checks.why: The mammalian diving reflex is strongest in children and cold water dramatically lowers metabolic demand, so intact survivals past 30 minutes are documented. Hypothermic arrest patients are resuscitated until rewarmed — not dead until warm and dead.

checks.q: At a trench collapse with a worker buried to the chest, your role as an awareness-level EMT includes:
choices: Digging by hand at the head end to free the airway
Entering with a shovel while a partner watches the lip
Keeping personnel and equipment back from the lip, shutting down machinery, and calling technical rescue
Backing the ambulance to the trench edge for quicker loading
checks.why: Secondary collapse is the leading killer of rescuers and is triggered by vibration and load near the lip. Entry without engineered shoring is prohibited, and parking the ambulance at the edge adds exactly the load that causes the next collapse.

lessons.title: Transport operations in depth: checks, driving, air medical and landing zones
lessons.body:
## The most dangerous thing you do is drive

### The daily check, by system

Do it at the start of every shift, in the same order, so nothing is skipped.

- **Vehicle:** fluids, tires, brakes, lights, wipers, fuel `3/4` or better, mirrors, warning lights, siren.
- **Communications:** radio channels, cell phone, mobile data terminal.
- **Oxygen:** a full **D** or **M** cylinder reads about `2,000 psi`; replace at or below `500 psi`. Check regulators, tubing, masks, cannulas.
- **Airway and suction:** BVMs adult, child, infant; OPAs and NPAs in a full size range; a suction unit that pulls at least `300 mmHg` with the tubing clamped.
- **Monitoring and AED:** pads in date (adult and pediatric), battery charged, self-test passed.
- **Trauma:** dressings, tourniquets, splints, collars in all sizes, board and straps.
- **Medications:** oxygen, aspirin, oral glucose, naloxone, epinephrine auto-injectors — all in date.
- **Infection control:** gloves, eye protection, gowns, N95s, sharps container not overfull.

### The nine phases of an ambulance call

`1` Preparation. `2` Dispatch. `3` En route to the scene, belted, roles assigned. `4` Arrival and scene size-up. `5` Transfer of the patient to the ambulance. `6` En route to the facility. `7` At the facility, verbal report and handoff. `8` En route to the station, cleaning and restocking. `9` Post-run: decontamination, fuel, back in service.

### Emergency vehicle operation

Lights and sirens ask other drivers for permission. They do not grant physics, and they do not grant legal immunity. The standard is **due regard for the safety of all persons**: an operator can be held negligent even when every exemption applied.

- **Intersections are the single deadliest place for an ambulance.** Most serious crashes happen there, usually involving a driver who never heard the siren. At every red light or stop sign: full stop, eye contact lane by lane, proceed one lane at a time.
- **Speed.** Stopping distance grows with the *square* of speed, so doubling speed roughly quadruples the distance you need, and an ambulance is top-heavy and rolls in evasive maneuvers.
- **Seat belts.** Providers in the patient compartment are the least-restrained people on the road. Belt in unless a task requires standing, secure loose equipment, and belt the stretcher at all four points plus shoulder straps.
- **Backing** causes a large share of ambulance collisions. **Use a spotter**, every time, with a signal that stops the vehicle if you lose sight of them.
- **Escorts** are dangerous: the second vehicle gets hit by drivers who pulled out after the first passed.

> **Trap:** "Lights and sirens" is a clinical decision, not a default. The time saved is typically only about `1-3 minutes` on a typical urban transport, which almost never changes outcome and multiplies crash risk.

### Air medical

Call a helicopter when time or access is the problem, not because the patient looks bad:

- Ground transport time to the appropriate center is prohibitively long (long distance, gridlock, island or mountain terrain).
- Prolonged **entrapment** in a critical patient.
- **Multiple critical patients** exceeding ground resources.
- A need for critical care capability during a long transport.

Limits: weather grounds aircraft, cabins are small and loud (reassess before you load — you cannot auscultate in flight), and there is a weight limit.

### The landing zone

- **Size:** `100 x 100 feet` for most medium helicopters; `60 x 60 feet` is a common small-ship minimum.
- **Surface:** firm, level, **slope under `5 degrees`**, clear of loose debris and snow that rotor wash turns into projectiles.
- **Obstacles:** clear of wires, poles, trees, and towers. Wires are the primary hazard and the hardest thing for a pilot to see — report them by position and height.
- **Marking:** one secured marker per corner; never loose cones, tape, or flares. Turn headlights and spotlights **off or away** at night.
- **Approach:** only when the crew signals. **From the front, in the pilot's field of view**, crouched, and **never from the rear** — the spinning tail rotor is nearly invisible and lethal. On a slope, approach from the **downhill** side, where the main rotor sits higher.
- Secure hats, sheets, and paperwork; everyone wears eye protection.

### Cleaning levels

**Low-level disinfection** handles surfaces touching intact skin. **Intermediate-level** handles visible blood or body fluid, using an EPA-registered tuberculocidal agent or a `1:10` bleach solution. **High-level disinfection** covers reusable equipment touching mucous membranes, and **sterilization** covers anything entering tissue — in EMS that is disposable. Clean the stretcher and high-touch surfaces after every patient.
keyPoints: A full oxygen cylinder reads about 2,000 psi; change it out at or below 500 psi.
Intersections cause most fatal ambulance crashes: stop, eye contact, proceed one lane at a time.
Due regard means lights and sirens never grant immunity, and they save only 1-3 minutes typically.
Always back with a spotter; belt in and secure equipment in the patient compartment.
Landing zone: 100 x 100 feet, slope under 5 degrees, clear of wires, approach from the front, never the tail.

checks.q: Which landing zone is acceptable for a medium medical helicopter?
choices: 100 x 100 feet, firm and level with under 5 degrees of slope, clear of overhead wires
50 x 50 feet of packed gravel with a single power line on one edge
150 x 150 feet of loose snow with road flares at each corner
A shopping center lot with cars parked to one side and a light pole at center
checks.why: The standard is roughly 100 x 100 feet, firm, level under about 5 degrees, and clear of obstructions. Wires are the leading hazard, flares and loose snow become projectiles in rotor wash, and a center obstruction rules a zone out.

checks.q: An ambulance running lights and sirens strikes a car in an intersection. Which statement is correct?
choices: Emergency exemptions grant immunity from liability
The other driver is automatically at fault for failing to yield
Sirens are audible far enough ahead that hearing is not a factor
The operator may be found negligent because due regard is still required
checks.why: Exemptions permit certain maneuvers but never waive the duty of due regard, so the operator can be liable. Sirens reach only a short distance ahead of a moving vehicle, and fault is decided on conduct, not on who had lights on.

checks.q: You must approach a helicopter with rotors turning. What is correct?
choices: Approach from the tail, since the main rotor is highest there
Approach only when signaled by the crew, from the front in the pilot's view, crouched
Approach from the uphill side on sloped ground
Approach immediately on landing to save time
checks.why: The crew controls approach, and the front keeps you in the pilot's field of view. The tail rotor is nearly invisible and lethal, and on a slope the main rotor is lower on the uphill side, so you approach downhill.

lessons.title: Terrorism, CBRNE and disaster response
lessons.body:
## Recognize, retreat, report

**Terrorism** is violence against people or property to intimidate a population or coerce a government toward a political, religious, or ideological goal. In the US the threat mixes international groups with domestic actors — single-issue extremists and lone attackers.

**CBRNE**: **C**hemical, **B**iological, **R**adiological, **N**uclear, **E**xplosive. Explosives remain the most common weapon by a wide margin.

### Recognizing a chemical release

You will not be told. You will arrive at a "multiple people sick" call and have to see it:

- **Many patients with the same signs and symptoms**, same place, no obvious trauma. The strongest clue.
- **Dead or dying animals, birds, and insects.**
- **Unexplained odors** — fresh-cut grass, garlic, bitter almonds, newly mown hay.
- **Low-lying vapor clouds, unexplained mist, oily films**, or a patch of dead vegetation.
- An abandoned sprayer, cylinder, or unusual device.

> **Key:** Multiple patients with the same toxidrome and no trauma means **stop, back out uphill and upwind, and report**. Your instinct to run toward patients is what the attacker counts on.

**Secondary devices** are placed to kill responders — at the obvious staging point, the approach path, or the entry doors. Stage upwind, uphill, and unpredictably; sweep the area; do not touch unattended packages.

### Nerve agents

**Sarin (GB)**, **soman**, **tabun**, and **VX** are organophosphates — insecticide chemistry, orders of magnitude stronger. They block acetylcholinesterase, so acetylcholine floods every receptor and the body pours out fluid uncontrollably.

**SLUDGEM**: Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defecation, Gastric upset, Emesis, Miosis (pinpoint pupils). Or **DUMBELS**, which adds Bradycardia, Bronchorrhea, and Bronchospasm — the B's are the killers, because the airway fills with secretions and clamps down. Seizures and paralysis follow.

After decontamination, treat with the **DuoDote** (ATNAA) autoinjector: **atropine `2.1 mg` plus pralidoxime chloride (2-PAM) `600 mg` IM** in the outer thigh, repeated per protocol, commonly up to `3` doses. Atropine dries secretions; pralidoxime reclaims the enzyme before it binds permanently. The endpoint is dried secretions and easier ventilation, **not** pupil size. Many services also carry **midazolam** for the seizures.

### The other chemical classes

- **Vesicants** — sulfur mustard (garlic odor), lewisite. Burns and blisters may be **delayed `2-24 hours`**, so a patient with no findings is not cleared. Decontaminate immediately.
- **Cyanide** — blocks cells from using oxygen. Rapid collapse, seizures, gasping, **red or normal skin with a normal pulse oximeter reading** in a dying patient. Antidote is hydroxocobalamin.
- **Pulmonary agents** — chlorine (greenish, pool-shock smell) and phosgene (mown hay), which causes **delayed pulmonary edema up to `24-48 hours`** later. Oxygen, keep them still, transport.
- **Riot control agents** — CS, OC. Miserable, rarely dangerous; fresh air and irrigation.

### Radiological and nuclear

A **dirty bomb** is conventional explosive wrapped in radioactive material; the blast, not the radiation, causes the immediate casualties. Protect yourself with **time, distance, and shielding** — dose falls with the square of distance. Alpha is stopped by skin, beta by clothing, gamma only by lead or concrete. Acute radiation syndrome starts with vomiting, and the **shorter the time to vomiting, the higher the dose**. Removing clothing removes about `90%` of external contamination.

### Biological agents

**Anthrax**: inhalational form starts flu-like and turns catastrophic; not contagious. **Smallpox**: highly contagious, rash on the face and extremities with all lesions at the **same stage** (unlike chickenpox). **Pneumonic plague**: contagious, rapidly fatal. **Botulinum toxin**: descending symmetric paralysis from the cranial nerves down, patient alert and afebrile. **Ricin**: blocks protein synthesis, not contagious.

A covert release announces itself **epidemiologically** — an unusual disease in an unusual season and age group, clustered among people sharing one location, plus sick animals — days later in a public health office, not on your call.

### Blast injury

| Phase | Mechanism | Injuries |
|---|---|---|
| **Primary** | The pressure wave | Air-filled organs: **tympanic membranes**, **blast lung**, **hollow gut** |
| **Secondary** | Debris and shrapnel | Penetrating trauma — the most common cause of death |
| **Tertiary** | Body thrown into objects | Blunt trauma, fractures, head injury |
| **Quaternary** | Everything else | Burns, crush, inhaled toxins |

Blast lung can be delayed and can worsen with positive pressure ventilation. Any blast patient with ear pain, deafness, or shortness of breath gets oxygen and a trauma center.

### Disaster, triage, and ICS

Disasters flip the standard from best care for each patient to **greatest good for the greatest number**. **START** sorts adults by respirations, perfusion, and mental status into Immediate (red), Delayed (yellow), Minor (green), and Expectant (black); **JumpSTART** adapts it for children. It all runs under the **Incident Command System**: one commander, a span of control of about `3-7` reports, one communications plan.

> **On the exam:** The EMT's role at a terrorist or CBRNE event, in order: **recognize** the indicators, **retreat** upwind and uphill, **report** to dispatch with a full description, **isolate** the area and keep others out, and **notify** the specialized resources. You do not enter a hot zone, and you do not treat contaminated patients before decontamination.
keyPoints: Multiple patients with identical symptoms and no trauma is a chemical release until proven otherwise.
Nerve agents produce SLUDGEM/DUMBELS; DuoDote gives atropine 2.1 mg plus pralidoxime 600 mg IM.
Secondary devices target responders: stage upwind, uphill, and away from the obvious spot.
Blast injury: primary hits tympanic membranes, lungs, and hollow gut; secondary shrapnel kills most.
Radiation protection is time, distance, shielding; removing clothing removes about 90% of contamination.

checks.q: You arrive at a subway platform where 20 people are vomiting, drooling, and have pinpoint pupils. Several are seizing. What is your first action?
choices: Enter and begin assigning triage tags
Back out upwind and uphill, report a suspected nerve agent, and isolate the area
Begin ventilating the closest apneic patient
Administer DuoDote to patients where they lie
checks.why: Many patients sharing one toxidrome with no trauma means an active chemical hazard and an unprotected rescuer becomes a patient. Recognize, retreat, report, isolate, notify comes first; triage, ventilation, and antidotes happen after decontamination in a safe zone.

checks.q: The DuoDote autoinjector delivers which two drugs and in what doses?
choices: Epinephrine 0.3 mg and diphenhydramine 50 mg
Naloxone 2 mg and midazolam 5 mg
Atropine 2.1 mg and pralidoxime chloride 600 mg intramuscularly
Atropine 1 mg and hydroxocobalamin 5 g
checks.why: DuoDote (ATNAA) is atropine 2.1 mg plus pralidoxime 600 mg IM for nerve agent or organophosphate poisoning. Epinephrine is for anaphylaxis, naloxone for opioids, and hydroxocobalamin is the cyanide antidote given IV, not by autoinjector.

checks.q: A bombing victim has ruptured eardrums and is short of breath with clear lungs on arrival. Which blast phase and concern?
choices: Secondary phase shrapnel; look for entry wounds only
Tertiary phase; assume a spinal injury and nothing else
Quaternary phase; treat for burns
Primary phase; suspect blast lung and give oxygen with a trauma center destination
checks.why: The pressure wave damages air-filled organs, so ruptured tympanic membranes are a marker of significant primary blast exposure and blast lung may develop over hours. Shrapnel, being thrown, and burns are the later phases and do not explain the eardrums.

cards.front: Why handle the neck gently in a patient with Down syndrome?
cards.back: Atlantoaxial instability: a lax transverse ligament in roughly 10-15% allows C1 to shift on C2, so low-force mechanisms can injure the cord.

cards.front: What airway features make Down syndrome patients harder to ventilate?
cards.back: Large tongue, small mid-face, short neck, and a narrower trachea. Consider an airway adjunct smaller than body size suggests.

cards.front: About what percentage of people with Down syndrome are born with a congenital heart defect?
cards.back: About 50%. Factor it into any chest pain, syncope, or respiratory complaint.

cards.front: Does cerebral palsy mean intellectual disability?
cards.back: Often not. CP is a movement disorder; many patients have normal cognition but hard-to-understand speech because the same injury affects speech muscles.

cards.front: How do you fit a patient with contractures onto a stretcher?
cards.back: Pad the voids and secure them in their position of comfort. Never straighten a contracture; the joint is fixed and forcing it causes injury.

cards.front: What does lack of eye contact mean in an autistic patient?
cards.back: Nothing about honesty or mental status. It is a feature of autism. Do not chart it as uncooperative or evasive behavior.

cards.front: Name four ways to lower sensory load for an autistic patient.
cards.back: Kill the lightbar and siren, dim the compartment, have one person speak in short concrete sentences, and allow the comfort object to ride along.

cards.front: Why is shouting at a hard-of-hearing patient counterproductive?
cards.back: Shouting distorts mouth shape and clips consonants, destroying lip-reading cues. Speak at normal volume, slightly slower and lower in pitch, facing the patient.

cards.front: Roughly how much of English speech can a skilled lip reader capture from lips alone?
cards.back: About 30-40%. The rest is guessed from context, so a nodding patient may have understood nothing. Confirm in writing.

cards.front: What assistive items should travel with the patient?
cards.back: Hearing aids and cochlear implant processor, glasses, white cane, service animal, walker, and any communication board or device.

cards.front: How do you guide a blind patient who is ambulatory?
cards.back: Announce yourself, offer your elbow, and let the patient take your arm and walk half a step behind. Never push or steer by the shoulders.

cards.front: Aphasia versus dysarthria: what is the difference?
cards.back: Aphasia is broken language from brain injury: wrong or missing words, possibly lost comprehension. Dysarthria is slurred articulation from weak speech muscles with correct word choice.

cards.front: How do you ventilate a patient with a laryngectomy?
cards.back: Through the neck stoma, with an infant or pediatric mask sealed over it or a BVM attached directly. The mouth and nose no longer connect to the lungs.

cards.front: What is the maximum suction time for one pass in an adult? In an infant?
cards.back: 10 seconds in an adult, 5 seconds in an infant. Preoxygenate 30-60 seconds before and reoxygenate about 30 seconds between passes.

cards.front: Do you apply suction while inserting the catheter?
cards.back: No. Insert without suction to the tube's length or a pre-measured depth, then apply suction while withdrawing and rotating the catheter.

cards.front: What does the DOPE mnemonic stand for?
cards.back: Displacement of the tube, Obstruction by secretions, Pneumothorax, and Equipment failure. Work it in that order when a ventilated patient deteriorates.

cards.front: First step with an obstructed tracheostomy tube?
cards.back: Remove the inner cannula. It is often the plug itself. Then suction, then consider ventilating the stoma directly.

cards.front: Cuffed versus uncuffed tracheostomy tube: why the difference?
cards.back: A cuff seals the trachea so a ventilator can deliver pressure without a leak. Uncuffed tubes let air pass to the vocal cords so the patient can speak; usual in children.

cards.front: High-pressure versus low-pressure ventilator alarm: what does each mean?
cards.back: High pressure means resistance: mucus plug, kinked circuit, biting, bronchospasm, or pneumothorax. Low pressure means a leak: disconnection, deflated cuff, or a tube that came out.

cards.front: What is the universal EMT move for a deteriorating ventilator patient?
cards.back: Disconnect from the ventilator and bag the tube with 100% oxygen at 15 L/min, then reassess. That removes the machine from the differential.

cards.front: A G-tube has fallen out. What do you do?
cards.back: Cover the site with a dry dressing, bring the tube, and transport. The tract can begin closing within hours; do not force reinsertion unless protocol allows it.

cards.front: What is the deadliest complication in tube-fed patients?
cards.back: Aspiration. Stop the feed, suction, and transport with the head elevated about 30 degrees or positioned on the side when possible.

cards.front: How do you position a patient with a suspected air embolism from a central line?
cards.back: Clamp the line, cover the site, place the patient left side down with the head lowered, and give high-flow oxygen. This traps air in the right ventricle.

cards.front: May an EMT use a patient's central line, PICC, or port for access?
cards.back: No. That is outside EMT scope and outside most paramedic protocols without specific training. Use a peripheral site or let the hospital access it.

cards.front: Where does a VP shunt drain, and what are the signs it has failed?
cards.back: From a brain ventricle to the abdomen. Failure: headache, vomiting, sleepiness or irritability, altered mental status; in an infant, a bulging tense fontanelle.

cards.front: What are the three components of Cushing's triad?
cards.back: Rising blood pressure with a widening pulse pressure, slowing heart rate, and irregular breathing. It signals dangerously high intracranial pressure.

cards.front: Which ostomy dehydrates a patient fastest and why?
cards.back: An ileostomy. Output leaves the small intestine before the colon reabsorbs water, so it is liquid and high volume.

cards.front: What is the weight rating of a standard versus a bariatric stretcher?
cards.back: Standard stretchers rate about 500-650 pounds; bariatric units rate roughly 1,000-1,600 pounds. Exceeding the rating drops the patient and injures the crew.

cards.front: Why does a too-small BP cuff read falsely high?
cards.back: It must be inflated to a higher pressure to compress the artery through surrounding tissue. The bladder should cover about 80% of arm circumference.

cards.front: Why transport a bariatric patient semi-upright rather than flat?
cards.back: Supine, abdominal contents press on the diaphragm and worsen ventilation. Obesity hypoventilation also means chronic carbon dioxide retention and a lower baseline saturation.

cards.front: What prognosis defines hospice eligibility?
cards.back: About 6 months or less to live if the disease runs its usual course, with curative treatment stopped. Palliative care has no prognosis requirement.

cards.front: What care may you still give a patient with a valid DNR?
cards.back: Everything short of resuscitation: oxygen, suctioning, pain control, splinting, bleeding control, positioning, comfort, and transport. A DNR applies only at arrest.

cards.front: How does POLST differ from a DNR?
cards.back: POLST (MOLST in some states) is a broader portable physician order covering CPR, level of intervention, artificial nutrition, and antibiotics. A DNR addresses resuscitation only.

cards.front: The DNR is missing or the family demands resuscitation. What do you do?
cards.back: Begin resuscitation and contact medical control immediately. You can stop resuscitation later; you cannot recover time lost to delay.

cards.front: What burn pattern indicates forced immersion in a child?
cards.back: A stocking-and-glove distribution with a sharp, level line and no splash marks, sometimes with doughnut sparing where skin pressed the cooler tub bottom.

cards.front: Why are bruises significant in a non-mobile infant?
cards.back: An infant who cannot roll, crawl, or cruise cannot injure himself. Any bruising in a pre-mobile child is a red flag for inflicted injury.

cards.front: How does abusive head trauma (shaken baby) typically present?
cards.back: An irritable, vomiting, seizing, or unresponsive infant with no external injury. Shaking tears bridging veins causing subdural bleeding and retinal hemorrhages.

cards.front: What is the most common form of elder abuse?
cards.back: Financial exploitation: missing checks, unpaid bills despite income, suddenly changed legal documents. Neglect is the most common physical form.

cards.front: How do you interview a suspected intimate partner violence patient?
cards.back: Separate the parties, usually by taking the patient alone to the ambulance. Ask direct non-judgmental questions, never confront the abuser, and never promise secrecy.

cards.front: What standard triggers a mandatory report of suspected child abuse, and what is the NJ hotline?
cards.back: Reasonable suspicion, not proof. In New Jersey report to the State Central Registry at 1-877-NJ-ABUSE (1-877-652-2873). Good-faith reports carry immunity.

cards.front: How should clothing be handled in a suspected sexual assault?
cards.back: Cut around, not through, holes and tears. Do not let the patient bathe, change, eat, or drink. Package clothing in a paper bag, never plastic.

cards.front: Name the six phases of vehicle extrication in order.
cards.back: Scene size-up and hazard control, stabilization, gaining access, disentanglement, removal and packaging, transport.

cards.front: What is the 5-10-20 inch airbag rule?
cards.back: Keep at least 5 inches from a side-impact airbag, 10 inches from a driver airbag, and 20 inches from a passenger airbag that has not deployed.

cards.front: What color are high-voltage cables on hybrid and electric vehicles, and what voltage?
cards.back: Orange, carrying roughly 200-800 volts DC. Never cut orange cabling. Damaged packs can enter thermal runaway and reignite hours or days later.

cards.front: What is the difference between simple and complex access?
cards.back: Simple access uses no tools: try every door, roll down a window, have the patient unlock it. Complex access uses hydraulic tools and trained rescuers.

cards.front: Which automotive glass can be punched out and which must be cut?
cards.back: Side and rear windows are tempered and shatter into blunt cubes when struck at a lower corner. The windshield is laminated and must be sawed or cut out.

cards.front: What are the three criteria for rapid extrication?
cards.back: An unsafe scene, an unstable patient you cannot manage in place, or a patient blocking access to a more critical patient. Nothing else qualifies.

cards.front: How many rescuers does the classic rapid extrication technique require, and who commands it?
cards.back: Three: one holding manual in-line stabilization at the head, one rotating the torso in eighth-turns, one moving the legs. The provider at the head calls every move.

cards.front: What are the three levels of technical rescue training?
cards.back: Awareness (recognize, secure, call for help), Operations (work at the edge of the hazard zone), Technician (enter and perform the rescue). Most EMTs are awareness level.

cards.front: What is the order of water rescue attempts?
cards.back: Reach, Throw, Row, Go. Only a trained, equipped swimmer enters. Wear a personal flotation device any time you work within about 10 feet of the water.

cards.front: Why resuscitate a cold-water submersion victim after a long downtime?
cards.back: The mammalian diving reflex plus cold slash metabolic demand, and intact survivals past 30 minutes are documented, especially in children. Not dead until warm and dead.

cards.front: What is the HELP position and when do you use it?
cards.back: Heat Escape Lessening Posture: knees drawn to the chest, arms pressed to the sides, floating still in a PFD. Used for self-rescue in cold water; swimming burns heat.

cards.front: Below what oxygen concentration is an atmosphere considered oxygen-deficient?
cards.back: Below 19.5% oxygen by OSHA definition; normal air is 21%. Confined space entry is permit-required and is never performed by awareness-level EMTs.

cards.front: How much does soil weigh, and why does that matter in a trench collapse?
cards.back: About 100 pounds per cubic foot, roughly 2,700 pounds per cubic yard. A buried worker cannot expand the chest to breathe, and secondary collapse kills rescuers.

cards.front: What separates low-angle from high-angle rope rescue?
cards.back: Low angle is under about 40-45 degrees, where the ground supports most of the load and rope assists. High angle is steeper, with the rope carrying essentially all the weight.
