cards.front: What pressure does a full oxygen cylinder read, and when do you swap it?
cards.back: A full cylinder reads about 2,000 psi. Replace it at or below 500 psi rather than carrying it as your working supply.

cards.front: Where do most serious ambulance crashes happen, and how do you prevent them?
cards.back: Intersections. Come to a complete stop at every red light or stop sign, make eye contact lane by lane, and clear one lane at a time before proceeding.

cards.front: What does 'due regard' mean for an emergency vehicle operator?
cards.back: Lights and sirens permit certain maneuvers but never grant immunity. The operator must drive with regard for everyone's safety and can be found negligent regardless.

cards.front: List four indications to request air medical transport.
cards.back: Prohibitively long ground transport time or distance, difficult terrain or access, prolonged entrapment of a critical patient, and multiple critical patients exceeding ground resources.

cards.front: What are the size and slope requirements for a helicopter landing zone?
cards.back: About 100 by 100 feet for a medium helicopter, firm and level with slope under 5 degrees, clear of wires, poles, trees, and loose debris.

cards.front: From which direction do you approach a helicopter, and which is never allowed?
cards.back: Approach only when signaled, from the front in the pilot's field of view, crouched. Never approach from the rear: the spinning tail rotor is invisible and lethal. Approach downhill on a slope.

cards.front: What are the strongest scene indicators of a chemical release?
cards.back: Multiple patients with identical symptoms and no trauma, dead animals or insects, unexplained odors, low-lying vapor clouds, oily films, and patches of dead vegetation.

cards.front: What does SLUDGEM stand for and which agents cause it?
cards.back: Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defecation, Gastric upset, Emesis, Miosis. Caused by nerve agents (sarin, VX) and organophosphate pesticides blocking acetylcholinesterase.

cards.front: What does a DuoDote autoinjector contain, and how is it given?
cards.back: Atropine 2.1 mg plus pralidoxime chloride 600 mg, intramuscularly in the outer thigh, repeated per protocol. Endpoint is dried secretions and easier ventilation, not pupil size.

quiz.q: A 6-year-old with Down syndrome fell from a swing and struck his head. Which anatomic feature most increases his risk of cervical spine injury?
choices: Atlantoaxial instability from a lax C1-C2 ligament
Fused cervical vertebrae
An absent odontoid process in all patients
Congenitally narrow spinal canal at L4
quiz.why: About 10-15% of patients with Down syndrome have a lax transverse ligament allowing C1 to slip on C2, so modest forces can injure the cord. The vertebrae are not fused, odontoid absence is not universal, and L4 is lumbar, not cervical.

quiz.q: An autistic teenager is rocking, flapping his hands, and repeating your last words back to you. The best interpretation is:
choices: He is having a psychotic episode
These are features of autism: stimming and echolalia
He is hypoglycemic
He is deliberately mocking you
quiz.why: Rocking and hand flapping are self-soothing stimming, and repeating your words is echolalia; both are autism features. Psychosis and hypoglycemia would bring other findings, and reading it as mockery leads to a punitive, escalating approach.

quiz.q: Your patient has cerebral palsy with fixed flexion contractures of both arms. How should you package him?
choices: Straighten the arms and strap them to the board
Apply traction until the elbows extend
Pad the voids and secure him in his existing position of comfort
Leave him unsecured so he can shift
quiz.why: Contractures are permanently shortened tissue; forcing extension causes fracture and severe pain. Padding around the patient's natural position is both safe and secure. Leaving a patient unrestrained on a moving stretcher is never acceptable.

quiz.q: You are assessing a deaf patient who nods after each of your questions. What is the most reliable next step?
choices: Continue; nodding confirms comprehension
Repeat everything more loudly
Ask the neighbor to translate
Write the key questions down and request an ASL interpreter at the ED
quiz.why: Nodding is a social response, not confirmation, and lip reading alone captures only 30-40% of speech. Writing gives accuracy now and an ASL interpreter gives it at the hospital. Shouting distorts the mouth, and a bystander is not an interpreter.

quiz.q: A stroke patient speaks fluently but the sentences are meaningless and he does not follow commands. This is best described as:
choices: Receptive aphasia
Dysarthria
Expressive aphasia
Intellectual disability
quiz.why: Fluent but meaningless speech with lost comprehension is receptive aphasia. Expressive aphasia preserves comprehension but blocks output, dysarthria is slurred speech with correct words, and intellectual disability does not begin abruptly.

quiz.q: A blind patient is able to walk to the ambulance. The correct technique is to:
choices: Take both his shoulders and steer him
Offer your elbow and let him hold your arm while walking slightly behind you
Ask him to follow your voice alone
Carry him to avoid delay
quiz.why: Sighted-guide technique lets the patient control contact and feel your changes in direction. Steering by the shoulders is disorienting, following a voice through unfamiliar terrain risks falls, and carrying an ambulatory patient is unnecessary and undignified.

quiz.q: You are suctioning an adult's tracheostomy and the pulse oximeter drops from 96% to 86% at 6 seconds. What do you do?
choices: Finish the full 10 seconds, then reoxygenate
Continue for 20 seconds to fully clear secretions
Stop suctioning immediately and reoxygenate with high-flow oxygen
Switch to a larger catheter and continue
quiz.why: Ten seconds is a ceiling, not a quota. Desaturation during a pass means stop and ventilate. Continuing, extending the pass, or upsizing the catheter all remove more oxygen from an already hypoxic patient.

quiz.q: A home ventilator patient becomes cyanotic. Chest rise is minimal and the high-pressure alarm is sounding. Your first action should be:
choices: Increase the ventilator rate
Begin chest compressions
Call the equipment company
Disconnect from the ventilator and bag the tracheostomy tube with 100% oxygen
quiz.why: Disconnecting and bagging removes the machine and circuit from the problem list in one move and lets you feel resistance directly. Changing settings is outside EMT scope, compressions are not indicated with a pulse, and phone calls do not oxygenate.

quiz.q: The 'D' in the DOPE mnemonic for a deteriorating ventilated patient stands for:
choices: Dehydration
Displacement of the tube
Dysrhythmia
Decompensation
quiz.why: DOPE is Displacement, Obstruction, Pneumothorax, Equipment failure — the four mechanical causes to rule out fast. Dehydration, dysrhythmia, and decompensation are not part of the mnemonic and do not direct an immediate airway action.

quiz.q: A child's gastrostomy tube came out 45 minutes ago. The site is clean with minimal drainage. What is appropriate EMT care?
choices: Reinsert a Foley catheter into the stoma to keep it open
Pack the stoma tightly with gauze
Cover the site with a dry dressing, bring the tube, and transport
Instill the scheduled feeding through the open stoma
quiz.why: The tract can start to close within hours, but reinsertion is a protocol-specific skill and a misplaced tube can enter the peritoneum. Covering and transporting is correct; packing and feeding through an open stoma cause injury and contamination.

quiz.q: Which set of vital signs best fits Cushing's triad in a patient with a failing VP shunt?
choices: BP 88/60, HR 132, RR 30 and regular
BP 190/70, HR 44, irregular respirations
quiz.why: Cushing's triad is hypertension with a widening pulse pressure, bradycardia, and irregular breathing — the body's response to rising intracranial pressure. Tachycardia with hypotension suggests shock, and the other sets are unremarkable or nonspecific.

quiz.q: A dialysis patient's central line cap is off and she becomes acutely dyspneic and hypotensive. Best position and intervention?
choices: Sit upright, oxygen by cannula
Supine with legs elevated, no oxygen
Clamp the line and place her left lateral with the head down, high-flow oxygen
Right lateral with the head elevated, clamp nothing
quiz.why: This is an air embolism. Clamping stops entrainment and left lateral head-down traps air in the right ventricle away from the pulmonary outflow tract. Upright and right-side positions speed air into the pulmonary circulation.

quiz.q: During assessment you notice a patient's stoma appears dark purple and dry. This finding suggests:
choices: Compromised blood supply to the bowel, an emergency
Normal appearance of a mature stoma
Dehydration only
The appliance simply needs changing
quiz.why: A healthy stoma is pink or red and moist. Dusky, purple, or black tissue indicates ischemia or necrotic bowel and needs surgical evaluation. It is not a normal or cosmetic finding and is not explained by dehydration alone.

quiz.q: You are called for a 420-pound patient with shortness of breath on the second floor. What should you arrange first?
choices: Immediate walk-down before he weakens
A bariatric unit and additional personnel before any movement
Placing him supine on the floor to assess
A helicopter for rapid transport
quiz.why: The move is the dangerous part and the plan must precede it: correct stretcher rating and 4-6 people. Rushing a dyspneic patient down stairs, laying him flat (which worsens breathing), or requesting aircraft for a non-time-critical complaint are all wrong.

quiz.q: A hospice patient with a valid POLST marked 'comfort measures' is in severe pain after a fall. What should you do?
choices: Nothing; the POLST bars intervention
Contact the hospice nurse line and provide comfort care, positioning, and transport if wanted
Begin CPR preemptively
Refuse transport and advise the family to call the funeral home
quiz.why: Comfort-focused orders describe the goal of care, not abandonment. Pain, positioning, and transport for symptom control are all consistent with it, and hospice has a 24-hour nurse. CPR on a perfusing patient and refusing care are indefensible.

quiz.q: Which statement about out-of-hospital DNR orders is correct?
choices: A DNR means no oxygen, no suction, and no transport
Family cannot revoke a DNR under any circumstance
When validity is unclear, begin resuscitation and contact medical control
A DNR takes effect the moment the patient is diagnosed as terminal
quiz.why: The default when documentation is missing, expired, or contested is to resuscitate and consult medical control, because care can be stopped but delay cannot be undone. A DNR withholds only resuscitation and applies at arrest, not at diagnosis.

quiz.q: A 4-month-old is unresponsive with no external signs of injury. The father says the baby 'just got sleepy.' What should you strongly consider?
choices: Abusive head trauma from shaking
Teething
Normal infant sleep cycle
Colic
quiz.why: Shaking tears bridging veins, producing subdural bleeding and altered mental status with no external marks. Teething, sleep, and colic never produce unresponsiveness, and a vague mechanism with a severely ill infant is itself a red flag.

quiz.q: Which documentation entry is appropriate for a suspected abuse call?
choices: 'Patient is a victim of child abuse by the stepfather.'
'Family seems suspicious and probably lying.'
'No comment; abuse should not be documented.'
'Circular 1 cm burn to left forearm. Mother states child "grabbed the stove." Injury noted 2 days old per mother.'
quiz.why: Documentation records observations, measurements, and quoted statements. Naming a perpetrator or recording your opinion is a conclusion you are not qualified to make and damages the case; omitting findings defeats the purpose of the report.

quiz.q: A woman has facial bruising and hoarseness after an assault by her partner. She minimizes everything while he stands nearby. What is your priority?
choices: Confront the partner so he knows he is being watched
Separate her for private assessment and transport, noting strangulation signs
Promise her nothing will be documented
Have her sign a refusal since she denies assault
quiz.why: Separation is the only way to get a private history, and hoarseness after assault suggests strangulation, which predicts later homicide and requires evaluation. Confrontation endangers her after you leave, and false promises of secrecy destroy trust.

quiz.q: Blue-gray flat patches over the lower back and buttocks of a healthy 6-month-old most likely represent:
choices: Fresh bruising from a belt
Congenital dermal melanocytosis, a normal birthmark
Petechiae from strangulation
Cellulitis
quiz.why: Congenital dermal melanocytosis (Mongolian spots) are flat, present from birth, and commonly mistaken for bruises. True bruises change color over days and are unusual over the sacrum in a non-mobile infant; petechiae are pinpoint, and cellulitis is warm and tender.

quiz.q: At a two-car crash, the driver is trapped with an undeployed passenger-side airbag intact in front of your work area. Minimum clearance to maintain?
choices: 2 inches
5 inches
20 inches
No clearance is needed once the engine is off
quiz.why: The 5-10-20 rule allows 5 inches for a side bag, 10 for a driver bag, and 20 for a passenger bag, which is physically the largest and most forceful. Stored energy in an undeployed module remains even with the engine and battery off.

quiz.q: A hybrid vehicle is on its side with an orange cable visible in the crushed rocker panel. Correct action?
choices: Cut the cable to de-energize the system
Pull the cable free before stabilization
Ground the cable with a metal tool
Do not cut or touch it; treat the battery system as energized and request fire
quiz.why: Orange marks high-voltage conductors carrying roughly 200-800 volts DC, and damaged packs can enter thermal runaway. Cutting, pulling, or grounding the cable can electrocute the rescuer or ignite the pack; isolation is done by trained crews.

quiz.q: Which describes correct vehicle stabilization before access?
choices: Cribbing and step chocks against the rocker panels, tires deflated to settle the vehicle
Chocking only the rear wheels and entering
Letting the driver hold the brake
Leaving the vehicle in gear with the engine running
quiz.why: Cribbing and step chocks transfer the vehicle's weight to a solid base, and deflating tires settles it so it cannot rock. Rear chocks alone allow rotation, and relying on a driver or a running engine leaves the vehicle capable of moving.

quiz.q: Which patient meets criteria for rapid extrication?
choices: A patient with a deformed ankle who is anxious about the tools
A patient with a decreasing level of consciousness and an airway you cannot control in the seat
A patient complaining of neck stiffness with normal vitals
A patient whose family is waiting at the hospital
quiz.why: An unstable patient whose airway cannot be managed in position meets the criterion. Anxiety, an isolated extremity injury with stable vitals, neck stiffness alone, and family convenience do not justify the increased spinal motion rapid extrication accepts.

quiz.q: A kayaker is clinging to a rock 15 feet from shore in moving water. You are an awareness-level EMT with a throw bag. What do you do?
choices: Wade out to him; the water is only waist deep
Swim to him with a rope around your waist
Throw the bag from shore while wearing a PFD and request a swiftwater team
Wait for him to let go and float to you
quiz.why: Reach, Throw, Row, Go orders attempts by rising risk to you. Throwing works from shore. Wading in moving water above the knee risks foot entrapment, and swimming with a waist-tied rope in current can drown the rescuer.

quiz.q: Two farm workers are unresponsive at the bottom of a grain bin. Your correct action is to:
choices: Enter quickly with a rope tied to your belt
Enter one at a time using an N95 mask
Lower an oxygen mask to them and enter to apply it
Stay out, secure the area, and request a confined space rescue team
quiz.why: Sequential collapse means an oxygen-deficient (below 19.5%) or toxic atmosphere. Entry requires monitoring, ventilation, supplied air, a harness, and an attendant. An N95 filters particles and supplies no oxygen, and a rope does not restore breathing.

quiz.q: A worker is buried to the waist in a 7-foot trench. Which action most reduces the risk of killing him or you?
choices: Keeping all personnel and equipment back from the lip and waiting for engineered shoring
Having two EMTs dig quickly while a third watches the wall
Driving the ambulance close to speed extrication
Using the backhoe already on scene to scoop soil away
quiz.why: Secondary collapse is the leading cause of death in trench incidents and is triggered by load and vibration near the lip. Digging without shoring, parking heavy vehicles at the edge, and running machinery all increase that load.

quiz.q: An 8-year-old is pulled from a frozen pond after roughly 20 minutes submerged. He is pulseless, apneic, and cold. Your action?
choices: Declare him deceased based on submersion time
Attempt one round of CPR and then cease efforts
Rewarm on scene fully before compressions
Begin CPR and continue resuscitation through transport
quiz.why: The mammalian diving reflex, strongest in children, plus hypothermia sharply lower oxygen demand, and neurologically intact survivals beyond 30 minutes are documented. Hypothermic arrest patients are not pronounced until rewarmed.

quiz.q: Your oxygen cylinder gauge reads 450 psi at the start of shift. What should you do?
choices: Replace the cylinder before going in service
Use it; anything above 200 psi is adequate
Top it off from a portable unit
Document it and use it for short transports only
quiz.why: A full cylinder reads about 2,000 psi and the working minimum before change-out is roughly 500 psi, because flow becomes unreliable at low pressure. Field topping-off is not done, and planning around a nearly empty cylinder invites running out mid-call.

quiz.q: You are backing the ambulance into a tight bay. The correct procedure is:
choices: Back slowly using mirrors only
Use a spotter with an agreed signal, stopping if you lose sight of them
Have a bystander stand behind the vehicle
Back quickly to minimize exposure time
quiz.why: Backing accounts for a large share of ambulance collisions because of blind zones mirrors cannot cover. A trained spotter in view, with a stop-on-loss-of-contact rule, is the standard. Bystanders are untrained and speed makes the blind zone deadlier.

quiz.q: Which is the strongest indication to request a helicopter rather than ground transport?
choices: The family requests it
The patient looks critically ill but the trauma center is 8 minutes away
A critical patient entrapped for a prolonged period far from a trauma center
The crew wants to stay in their district
quiz.why: Air medical is indicated when time, distance, or access is the limiting factor, such as prolonged entrapment far from definitive care. With an 8-minute ground transport, setting up a landing zone costs time. Family preference and crew convenience are not indications.

quiz.q: It is night and a helicopter is landing at your scene. Which action is correct?
choices: Aim spotlights at the landing zone so the pilot can see it
Mark the corners with road flares
Approach the aircraft from the tail as soon as skids touch
Turn headlights and spotlights away, secure loose items, and wait for the crew's signal
quiz.why: Lights aimed at the aircraft destroy the pilot's night vision, flares and loose items become rotor-wash projectiles, and the tail rotor is invisible and lethal. Approach only when the crew signals, from the front.

quiz.q: Twelve people in an office building have watery eyes, drooling, vomiting, and pinpoint pupils. Two are seizing. What is the most likely agent class and your first action?
choices: Nerve agent; withdraw upwind and uphill, report, and isolate the area
Riot control agent; enter and irrigate eyes
Opioid overdose; enter and administer naloxone
Carbon monoxide; open windows and enter
quiz.why: SLUDGEM with miosis and seizures is a cholinergic crisis from a nerve agent or organophosphate. Multiple identical patients means an ongoing hazard, so recognize and retreat precedes care. CS causes irritation without miosis and secretions; opioids and CO do not cause this toxidrome.

quiz.q: Why do responders stage in an unpredictable location upwind and uphill at a suspected terrorist bombing?
choices: To keep the media away from the scene
Because secondary devices are frequently placed to target responders at obvious staging points
To improve radio reception
Because the incident commander must be visible to the public
quiz.why: Secondary devices are deliberately placed where responders will predictably gather, along approach paths, and at entry doors. Upwind and uphill also protects against vapor. Media control, radio reach, and visibility are not safety rationales.

quiz.q: A patient exposed to a blast has ruptured tympanic membranes and progressive dyspnea 40 minutes later. What is the concern?
choices: Shrapnel wounds to the chest from the secondary phase
Burns from the quaternary phase
Blast lung from the primary pressure wave
Anxiety from the event
quiz.why: The primary pressure wave injures air-filled organs: eardrums, lungs, and hollow gut. Ruptured eardrums signal significant overpressure and blast lung can develop over hours. Shrapnel and burns would produce visible external wounds, and anxiety does not rupture eardrums.

quiz.q: Removing a contaminated patient's clothing eliminates approximately what proportion of external contamination?
choices: About 25%
About 50%
About 90%
Essentially none until full wet decontamination
quiz.why: Clothing removal is the single highest-yield decontamination step, removing roughly 90% of external contamination, which is why it precedes wet decon. Lower estimates understate it, and delaying all decon until a wash line is set up prolongs exposure.

scenarios.title: Rollover on the interstate, driver still in the car
scenarios.intro:
You are dispatched at 0210 for a single-vehicle rollover on the interstate shoulder. Fire and a rescue engine are `6 minutes` out. State police are on scene with one unit blocking a lane. Dispatch reports one occupant, a driver, still in the vehicle.

The vehicle is a sedan on its side against the guardrail, resting on the passenger doors. Traffic is still moving in the left lanes.

steps.prompt:
You pull up. There is a light fuel smell but no visible pooling. The car rocks slightly when the trooper leans on it. The driver is awake and yelling for help through the shattered driver's window, now facing up.

What is your first move?

choices.text: Climb up on the vehicle immediately to reach the patient through the window
choices.feedback: Wrong order. The car is unstabilized and rocking; adding your weight moves an unstable spine and can drop the vehicle off the guardrail with you on it. Nothing enters until it stops moving.

choices.text: Park in a fend-off position upstream, don your high-visibility vest, and size up hazards while fire brings cribbing
choices.feedback: Correct. Traffic kills more responders than the crash does. Blocking, visibility, and a hazard survey come before patient contact, and stabilization is the first physical task.

choices.text: Stand in the open lane and wave traffic around by hand
choices.feedback: Do not stand in live traffic. Vehicles and apparatus block lanes, people do not. This gets EMTs killed on highways every year.

choices.text: Wait in the ambulance until fire arrives in 6 minutes
choices.feedback: Too passive. You can safely park, protect the scene, gather information, and prepare equipment right now without approaching an unstable vehicle.

steps.prompt:
Fire arrives and cribs the vehicle solid in under two minutes. You can now reach the driver through the upward-facing window. He is a `34-year-old` man, restrained, alert, complaining of chest and neck pain. You can see an **undeployed side-curtain airbag module** still intact in the B-pillar beside his head.

What do you do about the airbag?

choices.text: Tell the rescue officer about it, stay at least 5 inches clear, and keep tools and personnel out of its deployment path
choices.feedback: Correct. The 5-10-20 rule keeps you out of a side bag's path, and the cutting crew must know before touching that pillar, which may contain the inflator.

choices.text: Strike the module with a tool to deploy it now so it cannot surprise anyone
choices.feedback: Dangerous. Deliberately discharging a bag injures whoever is near it, including the patient inches away.

choices.text: Ignore it; airbags cannot deploy once the crash is over
choices.feedback: False. Stored energy and capacitors keep undeployed modules live, and bags have fired during extrication.

choices.text: Place a folded blanket over the module and continue
choices.feedback: Well intentioned but not a control measure. A blanket will not stop an inflator. Distance and communication are what protect people.

steps.prompt:
You take manual in-line stabilization of his head and start oxygen. Over the next `4 minutes` he becomes quieter. His breathing is shallow and fast, his skin is cool and pale, and he now answers slowly and repeats himself. Fire estimates `12-15 more minutes` to cut the roof and do a proper packaged removal.

What now?

choices.text: Wait for the planned roof removal to protect the spine
choices.feedback: This patient does not have 15 minutes. Deteriorating mental status with hypotension and tachycardia is decompensating shock; waiting trades a survivable spine risk for death.

choices.text: Call for rapid extrication now: he is unstable, and get him onto a board with manual spinal control
choices.feedback: Correct. Falling blood pressure, rising heart rate, and declining mental status meet the unstable-patient criterion for rapid extrication. Speed is now the spinal intervention that matters.

choices.text: Pull him out by the arms yourself while fire keeps working
choices.feedback: The decision is right, the execution is not. Rapid extrication is a coordinated three-rescuer move with manual in-line stabilization and one person calling it, not a solo drag.

choices.text: Request the helicopter first and then decide
choices.feedback: Out of order. Aircraft do not resolve entrapment, and setting up a landing zone while a patient decompensates in a car wastes the minutes he has left.

steps.prompt:
Three rescuers perform the extrication. One holds the head, one rotates the torso in controlled eighth-turns, one moves the legs. He is on the board and onto the stretcher in `50 seconds`. In the ambulance his abdomen is rigid, breath sounds are equal, and a seat belt bruise crosses his lower abdomen.

The nearest hospital is `5 minutes` away. The trauma center is `18 minutes`. Choose your destination and transport plan.

choices.text: Trauma center, 18 minutes, with high-flow oxygen, warmth, and an early radio report alerting them to a hypotensive belt-sign patient
choices.feedback: Correct. A rigid abdomen with a seat belt sign and shock needs an operating room, which the community hospital does not have. The early alert buys them setup time.

choices.text: Nearest hospital, 5 minutes, since he is too unstable for a long ride
choices.feedback: Understandable, and defensible in an airway you cannot control, but this is bleeding. The closest hospital can only re-package and re-transfer him, adding an hour to surgery.

choices.text: Stay on scene to obtain a full set of repeat vitals and a detailed history before moving
choices.feedback: Harmful. This patient needs a surgeon. Reassessment happens en route.

choices.text: Trauma center with no radio notification to avoid tying up the channel
choices.feedback: Wastes your biggest advantage. The notification is what turns an 18-minute ride into a team standing in the bay when the doors open.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern: **stabilize before you touch, and let the patient's trend, not the plan, set the pace.** Everything early in this call was scene control — blocking traffic, cribbing, and identifying an undeployed side airbag with the 5-inch rule. Then the patient's numbers moved: heart rate up, pressure down, mental status down. That is the unstable-patient criterion for rapid extrication, and it overrides a tidy 15-minute roof removal. Rapid extrication is a three-person, one-voice technique done in under a minute, not a drag. Finally, a rigid abdomen with a seat belt sign and shock is internal bleeding, and internal bleeding goes to the trauma center with an early notification, not to the closest door.

scenarios.title: Multiple down at the train station
scenarios.intro:
It is `0745` on a weekday. You are dispatched to a commuter rail station for "several people sick on the lower platform." Dispatch adds that three more callers have reported people falling down near the escalators.

You are the first unit in. Your partner is driving.

steps.prompt:
From the top of the stairs you can see at least `10` people on the lower platform. Several are vomiting, several are on the ground, and one is convulsing. Two station employees who ran down to help are now sitting against the wall, drooling. There is no visible smoke, no fire, and no trauma.

What do you do?

choices.text: Go down and start triage tagging so the incoming units have a count
choices.feedback: Fatal instinct. Many patients with identical symptoms and no trauma means the hazard is still active, and the two helpers who went down are already symptomatic. You become patient eleven.

choices.text: Retreat from the stairwell, move uphill and upwind, and report a suspected chemical release with an estimated patient count to dispatch
choices.feedback: Correct. Recognize, retreat, report. Multiple patients sharing one toxidrome with no trauma is a chemical release until proven otherwise, and the sick would-be rescuers confirm the hazard is still present.

choices.text: Grab an N95 from the rig and go down to ventilate the convulsing patient
choices.feedback: An N95 filters particles. It provides no protection against a chemical vapor and no oxygen. You would be walking into the same exposure with a false sense of safety.

choices.text: Send your partner down for a quick look while you stay at the top
choices.feedback: Splitting the crew does not halve the risk, it just chooses who gets hurt. Neither of you enters an uncharacterized atmosphere.

steps.prompt:
You are back at street level. A station worker who was on the upper level walks over: pupils like pinheads, watery eyes, drooling, and he says he can't catch his breath and everything looks dark. He tells you someone left a plastic jug hissing near the far end of the lower platform about ten minutes ago.

How do you classify this?

choices.text: Riot control agent exposure; irritation only
choices.feedback: CS and OC burn the eyes and airway but do not cause miosis, drooling, bradycardia, or seizures. This toxidrome is cholinergic.

choices.text: Nerve agent or organophosphate: SLUDGEM with miosis, bronchorrhea, and bradycardia
choices.feedback: Correct. Pinpoint pupils, salivation, lacrimation, dim vision, bradycardia, and airway secretions are a cholinergic crisis. The 'dark' vision is miosis, and a hissing container fits a dispersal device.

choices.text: Carbon monoxide poisoning from a station generator
choices.feedback: CO causes headache and confusion with normal or dilated pupils and no drooling or miosis. It does not produce a cholinergic picture.

choices.text: Mass psychogenic illness given the crowd and the hour
choices.feedback: Anxiety does not constrict pupils to pinpoints, drop the heart rate to 52, or fill the airway with secretions. Calling objective physical findings psychogenic is how people die.

steps.prompt:
You notify dispatch: suspected nerve agent, at least `12` patients, hazmat and additional EMS requested, and request law enforcement for a secondary device sweep. The battalion chief asks you to pick a staging and treatment area.

What do you choose?

choices.text: The station's main entrance plaza, where everyone will naturally converge
choices.feedback: That is exactly where a secondary device would be placed, and it is downhill from the platform vent shafts. The obvious spot is the wrong spot.

choices.text: A location uphill and upwind, off the obvious approach path, visually swept for unattended packages before setting up
choices.feedback: Correct. Terrain and wind protect against vapor, and an unpredictable location off the natural convergence point protects against a secondary device aimed at responders.

choices.text: Inside the station concourse, out of the weather and close to the patients
choices.feedback: Indoors near the release means the same atmosphere, possible vapor accumulation, and no escape route. Treatment areas go outside, upwind, and uphill.

choices.text: The parking garage across the street, on the second level
choices.feedback: Better than the plaza, but an enclosed structure with poor egress and limited air movement is a poor treatment area and a hard place to receive ambulances.

steps.prompt:
Hazmat establishes decontamination. The first ambulatory patients are being stripped and washed. The station worker you assessed is now on the ground with copious secretions, worsening wheeze, and a heart rate of `44`. He has completed clothing removal and a wash line.

Your protocol authorizes DuoDote for nerve agent exposure. What do you do?

choices.text: Hold the antidote until his pupils return to normal size, then treat
choices.feedback: Wrong endpoint. Miosis can persist for days after systemic symptoms resolve. The endpoint for atropine is drying secretions and easier ventilation, not pupil size.

choices.text: Suction, ventilate with high-flow oxygen, and administer one DuoDote: atropine 2.1 mg plus pralidoxime 600 mg IM in the outer thigh, repeating per protocol
choices.feedback: Correct. The airway is what kills in nerve agent exposure. Suction and ventilation come alongside atropine to dry secretions and pralidoxime to reactivate acetylcholinesterase before it ages.

choices.text: Give naloxone 2 mg, since pinpoint pupils and respiratory depression suggest opioids
choices.feedback: Pinpoint pupils overlap, but opioids do not cause drooling, tearing, vomiting, bronchorrhea, or seizures. Naloxone does nothing here and delays the antidote he needs.

choices.text: Give the DuoDote but skip suctioning to save time
choices.feedback: Half right. The antidote is correct, but an airway full of secretions will not move oxygen no matter what drug is on board. Suction and ventilation are not optional.

steps.prompt:
Twenty minutes in, command is established under ICS and START triage is running. You have `4` red, `6` yellow, `9` green, and `2` black. Two hospitals are within `15 minutes`; a third is `30 minutes` out.

How should patients be distributed?

choices.text: Send all reds to the closest hospital so they arrive fastest
choices.feedback: This is how one emergency department gets overwhelmed and the second sits empty. Concentrating criticals at one facility degrades care for all of them.

choices.text: Distribute across all three facilities through the transport officer, reporting the agent and patient counts so hospitals can activate decon and antidote stock
choices.feedback: Correct. Distribution prevents overwhelming any one facility, and telling hospitals the agent lets them set up decontamination before contaminated walk-ins arrive at their doors.

choices.text: Let each crew choose its own destination to keep things moving
choices.feedback: Uncoordinated destination choice is exactly what the transport officer role exists to prevent, and it produces the same clustering problem.

choices.text: Transport all greens first because there are more of them
choices.feedback: Inverts triage. Greens are ambulatory and stable; they are transported last, though they do need decontamination and tracking so they do not self-present contaminated.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern: **a crowd of patients sharing one toxidrome with no trauma is a hazard, not a workload.** The single most useful thing you did on this call was not go down the stairs. Recognize, retreat, report, isolate, notify is the order, and the two station employees who collapsed while helping are the proof of why. The toxidrome itself is memorizable: pinpoint pupils plus wet everything plus a slow heart rate equals cholinergic, meaning nerve agent or organophosphate, treated after decontamination with DuoDote (atropine `2.1 mg` and pralidoxime `600 mg` IM) alongside aggressive suction and ventilation, titrated to dried secretions rather than pupil size. Then the scene-level thinking: stage where an attacker would not expect responders to gather, and distribute patients through a transport officer with the agent named, so the hospitals are not the next contaminated scene.
